          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following

I.A.No.119831 of 2025
1. We heard Mr. Gaurav Agrawal, the learned  Amicus, and
Mr. Kishan Chand Jain, the petitioner/applicant appearing in
person. We also heard Mr. Vikramjit Banerjee, the learned ASG
appearing for the Union of India.
2. This interlocutory application relates to Vehicle Tracking
System Devices. By our earlier order dated 13.05.2026, we had
issued a slew of directions as regards the Vehicle Tracking
System Devices.
3. In the note provided by the learned Amicus to us today, it
has been stated that the affidavit filed by the Union of India
is silent as regards the interaction undertaken by the Union
with the manufacturers of the vehicles.
8

--- Page 95 ---
W.P.(C)No.295/2012
4. We also take notice of the fact that some of the State
Governments have filed compliance affidavits as regards the
Vehicle Tracking System Devices.
5. In the aforesaid context, the learned Amicus prays for the
following: –
 
a) MoRTH may be directed to place on record the
report  of  its  interaction  with  vehicle
manufacturers regarding pre-fitment of VLTDs, as
directed in para 18 of the order of this Hon'ble
Court dated 13.05.2026;
b) All States/UTs may be directed to file compliance
status report qua enforcement of Rule 125H of
CMVR and measures proposed in the letter of MoRTH
dated 19.12.2025 
c) States/UTs may be directed, through their Chief
Secretaries, to take time bound effective steps
in compliance of Rule 125H. The decisions taken
and steps taken by the State Governments/UTs may
be placed on record by way of an affidavit before
this Hon'ble Court.”
6. In  the  aforesaid  context,  the  petitioner/applicant
appearing in person has also the following suggestions to be put
forward for consideration: –
“(d) the MoRTH may be directed to share, on a
monthly basis, District-wise and State/UT-wise
updated  data,  to  be  drawn  from  its  VAHAN
portal, of eligible public service vehicles
(PSVs) and their VLTDs fitment, in the public
domain to apprise the compliance status to all
9

--- Page 96 ---
W.P.(C)No.295/2012
concerned; 
(e) the  District  Road  Safety  Committees,
constituted under S. 215(3) of the MV Act, may
also be directed monitor this data and report
their initiatives to the National Road Safety
Board (NRSB) on a monthly basis; and that the
NRSB to place a consolidated report before this
Court on a quarterly basis;
(f) the  MoRTH  and  all  States/UTs  may  also  be
required to file their compliance status report
of the enforcement measures proposed in the
communication dt. 19.12.2025 of the MoRTH sent
to all States/UTs (filed as Annexure-14 of the
Reply Affidavit of MoRTH dt. 06.05.2026), which
proposed  actions  at  3  stages,  namely,  (a)
vehicle registration, (b) fitment and Pollution
Under  Control  Certificate  (PUCC),  and  (c)
permit under Rule 90 of the Central Motor
Vehicle Rules, 1989 and
(g) all States/UTs may also be required to ensure
that  every  VLTD-fitted  vehicle  is  (a)
registered in VAHAN with the device's Unique

and (c) transmitting live dual-IP data to at
least two servers as mandated by Section 4.2.2
of Automotive Industry Standard (AIS-): 140
including to National Emergency Response System
(NERS)/Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) for SOS
alerts in view of Rule 125H of the CMVR, which
applies AIS-140 to VLTD and Panic Button.”
10

--- Page 97 ---
W.P.(C)No.295/2012
7. We direct the MoRTH to place on record the report of its
interaction with the vehicle manufacturers regarding pre fitment
of VLTDs, as directed by us vide order dated 13.05.2026.
8. We also direct all the States/UTs to file compliance/status
report with respect to the enforcement of Rule 125H of  CMVR and
measures proposed in the letter of MoRTH dated 19.12.2025.

I.A.No. 77921 of 2024
12. The interlocutory application relates to speed governors,
as statutorily provided under Rule 118 of the Central Motor
Vehicle Rules, 1989 (For short, "The CMVR").
11

--- Page 98 ---
W.P.(C)No.295/2012
13. By  order  dated  13.05.2026,  we  had  said  that  all
manufacturers  are  duty-bound  to  fit  SLDs  at  the  time  of
manufacture.
14. We had also directed the Union to convene/have a meeting
with the manufacturers in this regard, and file an affidavit of
the Secretary, MoRTH.
15. As regards the aforesaid, thenUnion has filed an affidavit
stating that a meeting was convened on 30.06.2026 under the
Chairmanship of Chief Engineer (MVL) with (i) Society of Indian
Automobile  Manufacturers,  (ii)  Automotive  Component
Manufacturers  Association,  (iii)  International  Centre  for
Automotive Technology, and (iv)  Automotive Research Association
of India.
16. The stance of the Union is that in accordance with Rule 118
of the CMVR, 1989, speed governor can either be a Speed Limiting
Device (SLD) or Speed Limiting Function (SLF).
17. SLD is an on-board automotive device for restricting a
vehicle from going past its top set speed whereas SLF means a
function to control the fuel feed of the vehicle or engine
management in order to limit the vehicle speed to a fixed
maximum value.  
12

--- Page 99 ---
W.P.(C)No.295/2012
18. In the affidavit filed by the Union, a chart has been
provided highlighting which company provides SLD/SLF and at what
stage.
19. In the aforesaid context, we direct:-
(i) the Union of India to ensure that all
transport vehicles as required under Rule 118 of
the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 are sold

O R D E R
Heard Mr. Tushar Mehta, learned Solicitor General for the
appellant and Mr. Riwaj Rai, learned counsel for the respondent
No.8 in SLP© No. 498/2024.
2. Despite service of notice being complete on all the remaining
respondents, only respondent Nos. 1 to 8 in SLP (C) No. 498/2024,
respondent No. 1 in SLP (C) No. 27407/2023, Respondent No. 16 in
SLP (C) No. 27228/2023 and Respondent No. 20 in SLP(C) No. 499/2024
have entered appearance; however, nobody is present on behalf of
any of the respondents, except respondent No. 8 in SLP© No.
498/2024 when the matter is taken up and heard.
3. Leave granted.
4. The present appeals arising out of the common order dated
23.08.2023 passed by the High Court of Bombay in W.P.(C) Nos. 2443
of 2022, 1724, 1826 and 2355 of 2021 by which the liability to pay
gratuity to the private respondents has been fastened on the
appellant.
5. Learned  Solicitor  General  submits  that  the  Controlling
Authority before whom the matters were initially agitated held the
appellant liable to pay the gratuity despite being informed of the
fact that the appellant is not liable to pay the same and further
that it has no jurisdiction to decide the liability with regard to
the appellant.
6. He submits that as per Section 4 of the Gratuity Act, payment

--- Page 112 ---
5
of gratuity has to be made only to an “employee”, and the private
respondents who claim payment of gratuity were not “ employees” of
the appellant. He contends that there is no  employer-employee
relationship between the parties, and thus, the provisions of the
Gratuity Act are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of
the present cases. He further contends that, under Section 21(4) of
the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 ("CLRA
Act", for short), the responsibility for payment of wages would not
be on the appellant for the reason that it only talks about the
wages and not gratuity which is a separate component as per Clause
(vi) of Section 2 of the Payment of Wages Act, 1936.
7. Learned Solicitor General submitted that in the same Section,
it has been clarified that any gratuity payable on the termination
of an employee in cases other than those specified in sub-clause
(d) would not come under the definition of wages. He drew the
attention of the Court to Clause 12.4 of the contract between the
appellant and the  contractor, which relates to the terms and
conditions, specifically Clause 12.4.1, which clearly stipulates
that the said agreement is a job contract and does not create any
employer-employee relationship  between  the  appellant  and  the
employees of the contractor and further that this is a contract at
arm's length.
8. He further submits that even in law, the jurisdiction of the
Controlling Authority is limited to a dispute with regard to  the
amount of gratuity payable under the Gratuity Act and thus, the

--- Page 113 ---
6
question  of  deciding  the  liability  and  fastening  it  on  the
appellant was totally beyond its jurisdiction.
9. Learned Solicitor General refers to a recent decision of a
coordinate Bench of this Court in the case of the  Municipal
Council, represented by its Commissioner, Nandyal Municipality,
Kurnool  District,  A.P.  versus K.  Jayaram  and  Ors . dated
16.12.2025, which has clearly held that a person working under any
establishment, being sent there through a contractor, cannot claim
an employer-employee relationship with the principal employer for
whom he works, having been sent by the contractor.
10. Learned counsel for the respondent No. 8-Contractor, submits
that the liability does not rest on him, as whatever amount is
payable, ultimately has to come from the principal employer, which
in the present case is the appellant. 
11. Though there is no representation today before the Court, on
behalf of the other private respondents, but a counter affidavit on
behalf of respondents Nos. 1 to 7 is on record. The stand taken in
the same is basically harping on the fact that they had worked for
the appellant for a long period. However, on the issue which has
been discussed above, there is nothing to counter the submissions
of the learned Solicitor General.
12. Having considered the matters in their entirety and in the
facts and circumstances of the present cases, in our considered
opinion,  the  order  impugned  cannot  be  sustained.  We  are  in
agreement with the submissions of the learned Solicitor General

--- Page 114 ---
7
that the very maintainability of the proceeding in view of the
relief  claimed  before  the  Controlling  Authority  was  not
permissible.  The adjudication by the Controlling Authority with
regard to the liability was beyond its jurisdiction,  as the only
power conferred on the Controlling Authority under the statute was
to compute  the amount which may be payable to the concerned
“employee”. The Appellate Authority,  before whom  the appellant
succeeded, had rightly interfered in the matters and we find that
the reversal of the order of the Appellate Authority by the High
Court vide the impugned order was not justified.
13. Further, we find that under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936 as
also the CLRA Act, the contentions of the learned Solicitor General
are sustainable. Though the judgment in the case of The Municipal
Council represented by Commissioner, Nandyal Municipality, Kurnool
District, A.P  (supra) has been referred and relied upon by the
learned Solicitor General but we do not find any purpose will be
served by referring to the same at this juncture, in view of the
order we propose to pass.
14. Accordingly, for the reasons aforesaid, on the short point of
the Controlling Authority not being competent to go into the lis,
as was raised before it by the private respondents who had worked
through the contractor under the appellant, the appeal is allowed.
The order of the High Court is set aside and the order passed by
the Appellate Authority stands revived.
15. However, before we part, we observe that in the present

--- Page 115 ---
8
proceedings, the amount of gratuity claimed by the so-called
employees has already been paid to them by the appellant in terms
of the order of this Court dated 15.12.2023. Accordingly,  there
shall  be  no  recovery  made  from  them.  After,  clarifying  the
aforesaid position in law, the appeals stand disposed of.
16. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following

                             O R D E R
SLP(Crl.) Nos. 5756 and 5757 of 2026
1. At the outset, as requested by Mr. D.P. Singh, learned
Additional Solicitor General of India appearing for the Central
Bureau of Investigation (CBI), and Mr. Nizam Pasha, learned counsel
for the victim – complainant, SLP(Crl.) Nos. 5756 and 5757 of 2026,
which pertain to grant of bail/cancellation of bail to some of the
accused in Manipur violence cases, are ordered to be de-tagged. 
2. Post  these  matters  on  05.10.2026  alongwith  SLP(Crl.)
No.2729/2026 under different serial numbers.
Rest of the matters
3. Shri Dattatray Padsalgikar, former Director General of Police,
Maharashtra, appointed vide order dated 07.08.2023 to supervise the
investigation of cases by the SITs, has filed his 16th status
report dated 08.09.2026. The report highlights the law and order
situation subsisting from 01.08.2026 to 07.09.2026, inter alia,
noting that public protests were organised to update the NRC before
conducting the census in the State, which led to a 2-day shutdown
in  the  State,  followed  by  a  general  strike  for  two  days.
Thereafter,  the  State  decided  to  defer  the  census  before
implementing the NRC in Manipur, and the State Assembly also
reaffirmed  this  through  two  resolutions.  The  agitation  thus
subsided,  and  the  State  Government's  peace  initiatives  are
receiving a positive response. The initiative prompted two MLAs
from the Kuki-Zo Community to attend the Manipur Legislative
Assembly session in Imphal after a break of three years.
7

--- Page 129 ---
4. The road transport for public passenger services along the
Imphal–Dimapur–Guwahati National Highway No.2 has also successfully
resumed since 21.08.2026. However, there is an area where some
communal attacks continued to take place, resulting in the deaths
of three persons. The overall recovery of weapons stands at 8901
arms, 1,06,699 ammunition and 6390 explosives.
Status Report by CBI
5. The CBI has explained, as noticed earlier also, that there are
a total of 31 cases transferred to it for investigation by the
State Government, out of which charge-sheets have been filed in 28
cases before the Special Judge, CBI & NIA, Guwahati, as well as the
Chief Judicial Magistrate, Kamrup, Guwahati. Proceedings have also
commenced in all the charge-sheeted cases. Out of the total charge-
sheets filed, six were closure reports, four of which have been
accepted. Three cases are still under investigation by CBI. A total
of 978 witnesses have been cited, out of which only six have been
examined so far. There are 38 accused arrested in the matters.
Status Report of SITs
6. A  separate  chart-cum-status  report,  in  respect  of  the
FIRs/cases handled by the SITs, has also been placed on record. It
is pointed out that a total of 36 SITs of Manipur Police have been
constituted, and investigation by these SITs was monitored and
supervised by Mr. Dattatray Padsalgikar, former DGP, Maharashtra.
These SITs have been entrusted with 3020 cases for investigation,
out of which charge-sheets have been filed in 302 cases, closure
reports have been filed in 1583 cases, whereas 1135 cases are still
8

--- Page 130 ---
under investigation and trial has commenced in 33 cases.
Report by Three Member Committee
7. Report No.47 dated 14.08.2026 has been filed by the Three-
Member Committee headed by Hon'ble Ms. Justice Gita Mittal, former
Chief  Justice  of  Jammu  and  Kashmir  High  Court.  The  report
highlights mortality in the relief camps and the release of
compensation. The Committee has referred to a news item published
on 07.06.2026 in a newspaper stating that 25 internally displaced
persons (IDPs), sheltered in relief camps across Manipur, suffered
unnatural deaths. The Committee sent an email on 11.06.2026 to the
office of the Chief Secretary, Government of Manipur, seeking
information on the district-wise number of deaths in relief camps
since  03.05.2023.  Although  some  information  was  supplied  on
02.07.2026,  it  lacked  the  requisite  details.  Based  on  the
information so received, it was revealed that the Additional Deputy
Commissioner, Churachandpur, reported one unfortunate incident of
unnatural death resulting from sexual assault. Hence, another
request was sent to the State Government on 04.07.2026 to furnish
the information in the prescribed format. It seems that the
response to the communication dated 04.07.2026 is still awaited.
8. Substantiating the contents of Report No. 47 of the three-
member Committee, Ms. Diana Devi, IAS, who is working as a nodal
officer, has sent a response through email dated 17.07.2026, inter
alia pointing out that 640 deaths have taken place in the relief
camps across eight districts, out of which 34 are unnatural deaths.
The post-mortem was conducted only in 20 cases. Similarly, 25
9

--- Page 131 ---
criminal cases have been registered owing to unnatural deaths, but
investigation is complete only in four cases. No details concerning
the  remaining  cases  have  been  furnished  to  her.  The  report
shockingly highlights that the compensation amount paid to the next
of kin varies from Rs.20,000 to Rs.30,000 in some cases, to Rs.5 to
10 lakhs in others.
9. As the contents of the email dated 17.07.2026 sent by Ms.
Diana Devi speak for themselves, we direct the Chief Secretary of
the State of Manipur to file an affidavit explaining the details of
the deaths that have taken place in relief camps, especially in the
cases of unnatural death. It must be explained as to why post-
mortem was conducted only in 20 cases and not in all 34 cases.
Additionally, the reasons for such unnatural deaths, as per the
post-mortem report, should also be explained. The State Government
is also obligated to explain as to why, in some cases, a meagre
amount of Rs.20,000 to Rs.30,000 has been paid to the next of kin
of internally displaced persons who met with unnatural death while
they were sheltered in the relief camps.
10. We also direct the Manipur State Legal Services Authority to
take up this cause immediately to ensure that:
(i) FIRs are registered in respect of all the unnatural death
cases;
(ii) The cause of death, if unavailable, be adequately ascertained,
either from post-mortem reports or otherwise;
(iii)Identification of measures required to be taken to ensure the
safety and dignity of the internally displaced persons or other
10

--- Page 132 ---
vulnerable victims staying in the relief camps;
(iv) The expeditious and speedy investigation of the FIRs already
registered. 
The State Legal Services Authority shall also file a separate
status report in this regard.
11. In deference to our order dated 10.08.2026, the Manipur State
Legal Services Authority has filed a latest compliance report dated
15.09.2026. The report highlights the follow-up action taken by the
State Legal Services Authority. In para 9 of the report, the
details of the charge-sheeted CBI-investigated Manipur violence
cases have been furnished along with the name of the legal aid
counsel and his/her mobile number. The full description of the
victims and their legal heirs/family members is also given.
12. We have permitted the learned Advocate-on-Record for the
petitioners or other affected parties to note down the details of
the special trial numbers, the courts where such cases are pending,
and the legal aid counsel along with contact numbers. This will
ensure that if the victims or their family members need any further
assistance or there is any information to be furnished to the
defence counsel, it can be done without any impediment.
13. The Assam State Legal Services Authority has also filed a
separate compliance report highlighting the steps already taken to
comply with the directions issued by this Court from time to time,
and also as to how the Assam and Manipur State Legal Services
Authorities are acting in collaboration to ensure that all the
victims or their family members, etc., are provided legal aid
11

--- Page 133 ---
counsel and other logistical support for their participation in the
pending trials in Guwahati (Kamrup).
14. We may also note here that learned counsel have pointed out
the total pendency of cases before the Presiding Officer of the CBI
Court, who is also handling the NIA matters. This Court has, vide a
separate order dated 07.09.2026 passed in SMW(Crl.) NO.1/2026,
recommended establishment of two more NIA Courts in the State of
Assam for conducting trial in the cases of Section 11 of the
National Investigation Agency Act, 2008.
15. We are assured by Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, learned Additional
Solicitor General of India, that necessary steps to establish the
two additional Courts will be taken immediately. Once the needful
is done and NIA cases are transferred to the newly created Courts,
we have no reason to doubt that the Special Court in these cases
shall be exclusively assigned CBI matters for ensuring expeditious
trial.
16. Post the matters on 29.10.2026 for further consideration and
necessary compliance reports.

O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Interim orders dated 05.12.2025 and 16.12.2025 passed by the High Court of
Madras at Madurai Bench in WPCRL(MD) No. 2391 of 2025  are under challenge.
4. The saga of this litigation dates back to 1945, namely, a suit OS No.15/1945
was filed for various reliefs which ultimately culminated in a decree being drawn
under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) on 30.03.1946. As
per the said decree, six managers, three from Hindu Panikkars and three from
Christian Panikkars were empowered to manage the property of the Trust and
income flowing therefrom. It was also explicitly made clear in the said decree
1

--- Page 135 ---
that term of office of such managers would be five years and outgoing
managers would conduct elections for incoming managers and handover the
charge  to  them.  Originally  the  trust  was  named  as  “ Virudhunagar,
Thirumangalam,  Palayampatti,  KovilanKulam,  Periyakarisalkulam  Hindu,
Christian Panikar Community Trust ”. This was changed vide order dated
11.01.2017, which was also challenged in OS No.20/2012 and same came to be
dismissed  and  the  changed  name  of  the  trust  was  “ Virudhunagar,
Thirumangalam, Palayampatti, KovilanKulam, Periyakarisalkulam five villages of
Sriman Narayana Madam , Panikar Community of Paripalana Manging Trust ”.
The tenure of the last trustees, namely, the appellants herein, ended in August,
2021 and on account of fresh elections not having been conducted, the dispute
arose. It is stated that R Bhagavath Sing  and P Saravanan, Members of the
Hindu and Christian Panikars Community, have filed a suit in O.S. No.49/2023
against the trustees, including the appellants herein, seeking for a direction to
the defendants therein to convene a General Body Meeting to elect new
administrators to manage the property of the Trust and to appoint a Court
Commissioner to facilitate the process of election. Written statements are said
to have been filed and the suit is said to be pending. Be that as it may.
5. On account of there being a possibility of the peace and tranquility being
disturbed, the jurisdictional Tahsildar of Virudhunagar conducted a peace
meeting on 17.12.2025 wherein the parties are said to have agreed upon to
abide by the orders that may be said to have been passed in OS No.49/2023.
2

--- Page 136 ---
On account of wall posters and templates being circulated and demonstration
having been conducted by a particular group, the Deputy Superintendent of
Police, Virudhunagar, issued summons to the trustees, including the present
appellants, whereunder the parties were directed to workout the modalities as
per the outcome of the pending suit. It is at that juncture, the Respondent No.1
herein, is said to have submitted a representation to Superintendent of Police
seeking police protection during the General Body Meeting which was scheduled
to be held on 07.12.2025. A writ petition, namely, WPCRL(MD) No. 2391 of 2025
(Supra) came to be filed by Respondent No.1 herein seeking for a Writ of
Mandamus before the Superintendent of Police to consider the representation
dated 26.11.2025 to give necessary protection for the General Body Meeting
scheduled to be held on 07.12.2025. In fact, there is no mention or reference in
the writ petition about the pendency of the suit OS No. 49/2023. Appellants
herein also filed an Interlocutory Application to get impleaded as party-
respondents in the said writ petition and same is said to have been allowed. In
the said writ petition, the impugned order has been passed on 05.12.2025 by
appointing an Election Commissioner and ordering for election to be conducted
to the Trust in accordance with the decree dated 30.03.1946 passed in OS No.
15/1945 and further order came to be passed on 16.12.2025 by issuing certain
directions. Hence, these appeals.
6. Having heard the learned advocates appearing for the parties and on perusal
of the case papers, it would not detain us too long to set the dispute to a
3

--- Page 137 ---
quietus. A Perusal of the decree that came to be passed in scheme suit would
clearly indicate that first Committee of Mangers would hold the office for a
period of five years and fresh elections would be held once in five years and the
future  elections  shall  be  held  by  the  outgoing  Committee  of  Managers
themselves.  In paragraph 9 of the said decree, it is clearly and explicitly
indicated as under :
“9. The first committee of managers shall hold office for a
period of 5 years, and fresh elections shall be held once in 5
years. The future elections shall be held by the out going
committee of managers themselves. If within the period of 5
years, any membes cause to be one by reason of death or
any other cause, such vacancy shall be filed up in a meeting
of the community held as a whole. The list now prepared by
the commissioner shall be revised and additions made once
in every 5 years and before the election of committee of
managers  for  that  period  by  deleting  the  non-existing
panikkar member and adding the panikkar member who has
attained majority in the meanwhile.”
7. The present dispute seems to have arisen in the year 2021 when the then
existing Committee of Managers, who completed five year tenure, not having
conducted the election. The decree aforesaid is a complete answer to all the
questions raised not only in these appeals but also to all the disputes. We say
so for the simple reason that even the parties to the scheme suit, which
resulted in decree to be passed in wayback in the year 1946, were ad idem or
as to how to workout the future disputes. It was agreed upon by them that if
there were to be any difficulty in working out the scheme, any member of the
community (Whether Christian or Hindu) was entitled to apply to the Court for
suitable directions. The clause 14 as agreed upon between the parties reads as
under:
4

--- Page 138 ---
“14. If any alteration, variation or change in respect of this
scheme is found necessary and if any difficulty is felt in
working out this scheme, any member of the community
(Whether christian or Hindu) may apply to this court for
suitable directions. This court after notice to the parties on
record shall after hearing the objections, pass suitable orders
thereon. The application shall be made in this suit itself.”
8.  It  is  for  this  reason,  we  are  perforced  to  observe  as  to  the  very
maintainability of the Suit in OS. No.49/2023. However, we refrain from
expressing any opinion in that regard, since the parties to the suit are not
before this Court. As noticed hereinabove and at the cost of the repetition, it is
noted that remedies to the parties for redressal of their grievance would lie
before the competent civil court, which has drawn a decree under Section 92 of
CPC.
9. Though Mr. M.S. Ganesh, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellants,
has made a valiant attempt to contend that the provisions 0f the Hindu
Religious Endowments Act would be attracted, which at first blush, looks
attractive, by deeper examination of the relevant provisions of the Act, we
notice that said contention cannot be accepted. Section 3 of the said Act is
complete answer to the said proposition and the said act being applicable only
to the Hindu Religious and Charitable Trust and the instant trust being a
combination of both Hindu and Christians, the provisions of the said Act would
not be applicable. Even otherwise, the decree that has been drawn under
Section 92 CPC would prevail and govern the parties and it is for this precise
5

--- Page 139 ---
reason we have observed hereinabove that parties would be at liberty to move
the jurisdictional court, Virudhunagar, for appropriate relief including the
direction for conducting an election, if necessary, by appointing a suitable
person.
10. Hence, we permit the parties or any Member of the community to approach
the competent civil court which administers the scheme suits as contemplated
under section 92 CPC to seek such remedy as may be available to them and
reserve liberty in that regard. At the same time, a person who has been
appointed as a Manager much earlier and their term having been ended in the
year 2021, would not be entitled to continue in administration of the Trust.
There are various allegations and counter allegations made with regard to mal-
administration, mismanagement etc. It is not for this Court or the Courts
exercising the power under Article 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India to
examine such disputed questions of fact. It is also an issue which will have to be
thrashed out before the civil court, if necessary, by evaluating the evidence that
may be tendered by the parties in the scheme suit. At the same time, the
decree which has been drawn in the scheme suit, requires to be effectively
implemented for the betterment of the community at large. Any infraction or
deviation would defeat the very purpose of creation of such Trust and the
decree drawn.
11. Hence, we deem it proper and appropriate to appoint a Receiver to
6

--- Page 140 ---
administer, manage and preserve the Trust and its properties until and unless a
duly constituted body is elected under the supervision of the jurisdictional civil
court. Hence, we hereby appoint Justice as a Receiver of  Virudhunagar,
Thirumangalam, Palayampatti, KovilanKulam, Periyakarisalkulam five villages of
Sriman Narayana Madam , Panikar Community of Paripalana Manging Trust  and
the existing trustees who are now managing the properties of the trust, shall
forthwith  handover  the charge and the Receiver  shall take  charge and
administer the trust in the manner he/she deems fit and the receiver would be
at liberty to seek such orders or directions as deem fit in the proper
administration of the Trust from the jurisdictional civil court which has passed
the decree in OS No.15/1945.
12. In the light of the aforesatated order, the impugned order which directs the
appointment of an Election Commissioner and the order dated 16.12.2025,
issuing directions  would not be sustainable and it is  hereby set aside.
Accordingly, the appeals stand disposed of. No order as to costs.
13. In the light of the aforesaid observations, the jurisdictional High Court shall
pass appropriate orders for consigning the writ petition(s) to records.
7

--- Page 141 ---
14. All pending application(s) stands consigned to records.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
Civil Appeal No(s).12893/2026
@ SLP (C) No. 17918/2026
PUNJAB NATIONAL BANK                               Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
NIPUL CHANDRA DAS & ANR.                           Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal impugns the judgment and order of the Gauhati
High Court dated 13.02.2026 by which the Division Bench of
the High Court set aside the order dated 16.10.2025 passed
by the learned Single Judge in W.P. (C) No. 2291/2020 and
restored the award dated 20.11.2019 passed by Central
Government Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour Court, Guwahati
(for short, the Tribunal) in Reference Case No. 03/2019.
4. The first respondent, a class-IV employee in the appellant-
bank, was proceeded for misconduct. In the domestic inquiry
he was found guilty of the charges and was awarded the
punishment of dismissal from service  vide order dated
1

--- Page 145 ---
19.06.2017.  Consequently,  the  respondent  raised  an
industrial dispute which was referred for adjudication to
the Tribunal, and was registered as Reference Case No.
03/2019.
5. The Tribunal framed multiple issues including the one as to
whether the domestic inquiry against the workman was fair
and proper.
6. The management filed its written statement claiming that
domestic inquiry was initiated and conducted as per laid
down procedure but failed to produce the relevant records
of disciplinary proceedings and even failed to cross-
examine the workman witness. In consequence, the Tribunal
passed an award declaring the dismissal from service bad in
law and the respondent-workman entitled to reinstatement
with full back-wages.
7. Aggrieved by the award of the Tribunal, the appellant
preferred a writ petition before the learned Single Judge
of the High Court. The learned Single Judge  vide order
dated 16.10.2025 set aside the award passed by the Tribunal
and remanded the matter to the Tribunal. The operative
portion of the order passed by the learned Single Judge is
found in paragraph 13 of its judgment, which is reproduced
herein below:
2

--- Page 146 ---
“13.  Accordingly,  the  instant  writ
petition  stands  disposed  of  with  the
following observations and directions
(i) The award dated 20.11.2019 passed in
Reference Case No.3/2019 stands set aside
and quashed.
(ii)  The  learned  Central  Government
Industrial  Tribunal-cum-Labour  Court,
Guwahati,  Assam  is  directed  to  decide
afresh the Reference Case No.3/2019 from
the stage of providing opportunity to both
the parties to adduce evidence.
(iii) Taking into account that both the
parties are duly represented, they are
directed  to  appear  before  the  learned
Central  Government  Industrial  Tribunal-
cum-Labour Court, Guwahati, on 01.12.2025.
(iv)  The  Registry  of  this  Court  is
directed forthwith to remit the records to
the learned Central Government Industrial
Tribunal-cum-Labour Court, Guwahati, Assam
so that the records are available on the
next date.
(v) The observations and findings made in
the present order shall not affect either
of the parties in the proceedings before
the learned Central Government Industrial
Tribunal-cum-Labour  Court,  Guwahati,
Assam.”
8. The learned Single Judge set aside the order on the ground
that the Tribunal though framed multiple issues did not
deal properly with any of them. Besides having held the
domestic inquiry to be vitiated for want of production of
records relating thereto, the Tribunal ought to have given
opportunity to the employer to prove the charges by leading
evidence.
9. Aggrieved by the order of the learned Single Judge, the
respondent-workman preferred an intra-court appeal before
the Division Bench which came to be allowed by the impugned
order. The Division Bench proceeded to allow the appeal
3

--- Page 147 ---
primarily on the ground that if the management had failed
to even cross-examine the workman witness and produce
records to substantiate its case, no further opportunity
need be given to them. Accordingly, the order of the
learned Single Judge was set aside, and the award was
restored.
10. Assailing the order passed by the Division Bench, the
learned counsel for the appellant submitted that once the
Tribunal had framed the issue as to whether domestic
inquiry against the workman was fair and proper, the same
out to have been decided as a preliminary issue and if it
was  found  that  domestic  inquiry  was  not  proper,  an
opportunity to prove the charges ought to have been given
to the management. In absence of such opportunity, the
learned Single Judge was justified in setting aside the
award and remanding the matter back to the Tribunal for a
fresh consideration from the stage of allowing the parties
to lead evidence.
11. Per  contra,  learned counsel for the respondent submitted
that there was sufficient material produced from the side
of the workman to indicate that the charges were mala fide
and that there was no evidence to substantiate those
charges. Besides, when after filing the written statement,
the management had not participated in the proceedings, the
4

--- Page 148 ---
Tribunal  had  no  option  but  to  pass  an  award  of
reinstatement based on uncontroverted testimony of the
workman.
12. We have accorded due consideration to the rival contentions
and have perused the record. 
13. The statement of claim preferred by the workman before the
Tribunal reveals that the workman was served with a charge
sheet and a domestic inquiry was held. Paragraphs 10 to 16
of the statement of claim are reproduced below:
“10. That the Workman had replied to the
issued  Charge  Sheet  dated  05.01.2017
denying the charges that the charges are
totally fabricated, exaggerated, distorted
and  concocted.  The  argument  with  the
Manager over running of Generator whole
night  has  exaggerated  unnecessarily  to
take revenge of some hidden activities of
the  Branch….  at  9.30  AM,  no  one  was
present in the Branch premises and the
written  statement  given  are  under
coercion, duress and Intimidation... an
unblemished  service  record  except  this
one...Considering the above arguments and
his past unblemished record, he may kindly
be exonerated from the alleged charges. 
11.  That  the  Opposite
Party/Management,  having  not  satisfied
with the reply to the charge Sheet of the
Applicant/Workman,  appointed  Enquiry
Officer and Presenting Officer at their
own choice without issuing prior notice to
the Workman to collect a favourable Enquiy
Report.
12.  The  Enquiry  Officer  conducted  his
enquiry with a preconceived attitude which
is reflected in his Report. The Enquiry
Officer did not analyze the document ME6
in his report. The ME 6 was documented by
the Presenting Officer as a reply of ME5
which was not addressed to the Officer who
issued  order  for  explanation  to  the
Workman.  The  Enquiry  Officer  failed  to
note it in his Report.Further, the Enquiry
Officer  did  not  enter  into  the  cross
5

--- Page 149 ---
analysis of the filed documents between
ME-5 and ME 4, ΜΕ 7, ΜΕ 8, ΜΕ 9, ΜΕ 10 and
ME-11.  The  Enquiry  Officer  failed  to
notice/  record  that  placement  of  the
documents before the Applicant/Workman is
far from the date of forceful ouster and
suspension from service. Even ignored the
composition of ingredients of the Order
for  explanation  (ME-5)  and  the  Charge
Sheet(Ex-1)  findings/conclusion  of  the
Enquiry  Officer in  regard to  ME 4  is
injudicious in absence of admission of the
signatories in the proceeding.
13. That the Applicant/Workman had filed
his objection against the Report of the
Enquiry  Officer  as  asked  for  by  the
Opposite  Party/Management  claiming  that
the  EO  has  taken  a  biased  and
unjustifiable stand to prove the charges
against the Applicant/Workman.
14. That the Opposite Party/Management had
issued letter dated 31.05.2017 calling for
a  personal  hearing  of  the  Applicant/
Workman  on  the  matter  of  proposed
punishment.  In  the  said  letter,  the
Opposite  Party,  while  referred  detail
contents  of  all  documents  recorded  in
Enquiry proceeding, carefully avoided the
detail narration of the documents marked
as ME-5 and ME-6.
Further, the Opposite Party/Management had
arrived at opinion without any conclusive
findings of the Enquiry Officer that the
Applicant/Workman is a habitual offender.
15.  That  in  the  personal  hearing  on
16.06.2017 at Bank's Head Office, Kolkata,
the  Applicant/Workman  stated  that  the
incident (occurred on 26.10.2016) was a
spur of the moment reaction (resulted into
argument)
16.  That  the  submission  of  the
Applicant/Workman made in personal hearing
did  not  consider  by  the  Opposite
Party/Management and passed a final Order
of  Dismissal  from  service  vide  letter
dated 19.06.2017 with retrospective effect
of suspension dated 31.10.2016.”
14. From a perusal of the statement of claim it appears an
inquiry into the charges was held and documents were
produced.  Even  personal  hearing  was  afforded  to  the
workman. In such a scenario, even if we assume that for
some reason the inquiry was vitiated, the Tribunal ought to
6

--- Page 150 ---
have given opportunity to the employer to lead evidence to
prove the charges.
 
15. It is settled that where inquiry is found vitiated for
violation of principles of natural justice or for any other
reason, the employer must get opportunity to justify the
action  before  the  Tribunal  by  leading  evidence. 1
Admittedly, this procedure was not adopted. Therefore, the
learned Single Judge was justified in setting aside the
award and remanding the matter back to the Tribunal to
carry out the proceedings from the stage where the fault
had occurred.
16. In such circumstances, we are of the view that the Division
Bench erred in law by setting aside the order passed by the
learned  Single  Judge  and  restoring  the  award  of  the
Tribunal.
17. Consequently, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order
of the Division Bench of the High Court is set aside. The
order  passed  by  the  learned  Single  Judge  is  hereby
restored.
18. It is made clear that we have not expressed any opinion on
1 1 Workmen v. Motipur Sugar Factory (P) Ltd., AIR 1965 SC 1803, paragraph 11; Workmen 
v. Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. of India (P) Ltd. (1973) 1 SCC 813, paragraph 32 (4); State of 
Uttarakhand & Others v. Sureshwati, (2021) 3 SCC 108, paragraph 18.
7

--- Page 151 ---
the merits of the charges levelled against the respondent.
 
19. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

O R D E R
Heard Mr. Ajit Kumar Sinha, learned Senior Counsel
for the petitioner and Mr. S. Gowthaman, learned counsel
for the respondent.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeals arise out of a common order
dated 05.03.2025 passed by the learned Single Judge of
the High Court of Judicature at Madras in CRL.R.C.(MD)
Nos.488/2021 and 489/2021, by which, the judgment and
order of the Trial Court as well as the Appellate Court
were set aside and the matter was remitted back to the
Appellate Court with a direction to rehear the matter
and reverse the findings of the Trial Court and dispose
of the appeal in accordance with law.
4. Learned Senior Counsel for the appellant submitted
1

--- Page 169 ---
that the appellant has been wrongly made an accused in
the criminal case, which arose out of a pure accident in
which there was absolutely no criminal culpability of
the appellant, who was the owner of the factory. It was
submitted that even otherwise, the deceased was the
personal driver of the appellant and not a workman of
the factory. However, he submitted that the widow of the
deceased  was  given  a  compensation  of  Rs.5,00,000/-
(Rupees Five Lakhs) by the appellant, which she has
admitted  by  filing  an  affidavit  in  the  present
proceedings. Thus, learned Senior Counsel submitted that
on humanitarian grounds, as the deceased had served the
appellant, he is ready to pay a further substantial
amount  to  the  widow  of  the  deceased  so  that  her
financial requirements are taken care of to a great
extent. It was submitted that the appellant would also
explore the possibility of whether any of the dependents
can be rehabilitated by providing employment, which
would help the family to survive.
5. Having considered the matter, in our considered
view, ends of justice would be served if the appellant
discharges his duty as a model, humane and compassionate
employer to compensate the widow of the deceased and his
family adequately, both monetarily and if possible, by
2

--- Page 170 ---
also providing a job to the dependent member of the
deceased’s family, so that the family has some longtime
means to fall back upon.
6. In  our  considered  opinion,  in  the  facts  and
circumstances  of  the  case,  the  acquittal  of  the
appellant by the Trial Court, as confirmed by the
Appellate Court, was just and proper and needed no
interference.
7. Accordingly,  at  this  stage,  the  common  order
impugned is set aside. The judgment dated 26.12.2017
passed by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Karur, in
S.T.C.No.14/2017 stands confirmed. The appellant stands
acquitted. However, the appeals are kept pending as the
appellant has filed I.A. No.263107 of 2026 seeking
impleadment of the widow of the decreased as party
respondent no.2.
8. In the facts and circumstances of the case, I.A.
No. 263107 of 2026 is allowed in terms of the prayer
made.  The  widow  of  the  deceased  is  impleaded  as
respondent no.2 in the present proceedings. Cause title
be amended accordingly. Registry is directed to issue
notice to the newly impleaded respondent no.2.
9. List on 07.10.2026.
10. On  the  next  date  of  listing,  learned  Senior
3

--- Page 171 ---
Counsel for the appellant shall take instructions and be
prepared with the further offer, both in monetary terms
and, if possible, by way of providing a job also to an
eligible member of the deceased’s family.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.                              OF 2026
(@SLP(C) NO(S). 38502-38503 OF 2025)
DILIP SINGH RATHOD ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ORS.   ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard. Leave granted.
2. Facts in brief which led to the filing of the present appeals can be
crystallized as under:
State of Madhya Pradesh advertised for the recruitment of Patwaris
for which the appellant applied, cleared the examination and he was
included in the select list. During the counseling, the verification of the
documents took place and it was found that certificate of diploma in
computer-application, relied upon by the appellant, was from Chhattisgarh
University, Raipur, which was not recognized or it lacked UGC registration.
Consequently, the employment offered to the appellant was denied.
Aggrieved by this action, the appellant approached the jurisdictional High
Court in W.P. No.7717/2011, which petition came to be disposed of on
28.11.2011  directing  the  Collector,  Morena,  to  reconsider  the
representation and thereafter by a speaking order, the appellant’s
representation came to be rejected by order dated 30.06.2012.
1

--- Page 176 ---
3. Appellant claims that said endorsement or rejection order along with
other documents, were furnished to his counsel Shri Raj Kumar Goyal to
file a writ petition and he failed to file writ petition and in spite of repeated
follow up, the counsel misled him to believe that writ petition had been
filed and was pending. Counsel for the appellant, during the course of his
arguments before this Court, also relied upon an affidavit said to have
been filed by the said counsel whereunder he had deposed that he would
be taking steps to file the writ petition. In fact, this affidavit cuts the case
of the appellant. We say so for the simple reason that at one breath the
appellant says that said counsel who was entrusted with papers to file Writ
Petition was furnishing false date of hearing of the writ petition which had
already been filed and in the same breath he relies upon the affidavit of
previous counsel which would disclose that counsel had only assured the
filing of the writ petition or in other words admit that writ petition itself
had not been filed. Either of the two statements ought to be false.
4.  Be that as it may. The appellant is said to have filed a complaint before
the Madhya Pradesh Bar Council against the aforesaid advocate, which
came to be registered as Complaint No.90/2017 and it is stated that no
action was taken pursuant to the said complaint. Subsequently, the
aforesaid writ petition was filed, which came to be dismissed vide order
dated 01.08.2024 on the ground of delay and laches and aggrieved by the
said order, an intra-court appeal was filed in the Writ Appeal
No.2111/2024, which also came to be dismissed vide order dated
02.12.2024 and review petition filed thereon came to be dismissed on
25.07.2025. Hence, these appeals.
5. It is the contention of the learned counsel appearing for the appellant
that writ petition having been dismissed only on the ground of delay, same
be set aside and matter be remitted back to the learned Single Judge or
the Division Bench for adjudicating the same on merits as the appellant
2

--- Page 177 ---
has very good case on merits.  He would rely upon a Division Bench’s
judgment of the High Court rendered in Writ Appeal No.488 of 2012 to
contend that in identical circumstances, a similar prayer was granted and
respondents therein were directed to accept the diploma certificate similar
to the one relied upon by the appellant herein. Hence, it is contended that
appellant stands on the same footing and as such he cannot be deprived
of his valuable right. Per contra, learned counsel appearing for the
respondents would support the impugned orders.
6. Having heard the learned advocates appearing for the parties and after
bestowing our careful and anxious consideration to the rival contentions
raised at the Bar, we notice that order/endorsement dated 30.06.2012,
which came to be issued by the Collector, Morena was challenged in the
writ petition and it came to be dismissed on the ground of delay and
laches. At this juncture, we notice that no litigant would stand to benefit in
approaching the court belatedly. The delay when pitted against substantial
justice, necessarily the delay deserves to be condoned as it has to yield
before substantial justice. The Courts are respected not because they have
the power to punish but they have the power to undo the injustice that
might have crept in. These salutary principles when kept in mind and facts
on hand are examined, it would not detain us for too long to brush aside
the contention of the learned counsel for the appellant.  We say so for
reasons more than one. In the instant case, the delay seems to be have
occurred in three stages. In compliance with the order passed by the High
Court on 28.11.2011 in Writ Petition No. 7717/2011, directing the
Collector, Morena, to reconsider the representation, the prayer of the
petitioner was examined and, by a speaking order dated 30.06.2012, the
representation of the petitioner was rejected. The petitioner did not take
immediate steps to challenge the said speaking order of the Collector. On
the other hand, he claims to have entrusted or handed over all the
documents to an advocate for filing a writ petition and claims that, from
2012 to 2018, he was repeatedly following up with the counsel and was
3

--- Page 178 ---
misled to believe that writ petition had been filed and it was pending.
However, no attempts were made by the petitioner to ascertain the case
number or the status of the case for six years. This is the first stage of
delay. It requires to be noticed at this juncture itself that post to which the
petitioner had applied was that of Patwari (Keeper of Revenue Records).
Such a candidate is expected to exercise due diligence in pursuing his own
cause. If, at all, he had submitted the documents to the learned counsel in
2012, it cannot be believed that he would have kept quiet for six years
without ascertaining the details of his case from the counsel. The
petitioner also claims that his counsel gave a notarised affidavit assuring
him that steps would be taken to file the petition. The said affidavit is
dated 14.10.2016. The writ petition had not been filed at least till said
date. Petitioner could have taken steps to file a writ petition challenging
the speaking order dated 30.06.2012, which he did not do. This is the
second stage of delay.  The appellant has been moving even the
jurisdictional Bar Council and the consumer court against the advocate
who is said to have not extended the services or there has been deficient
services. When he has been pursuing those remedies, it is hard to believe
that appellant would have kept quiet in not pursuing his legitimate claim
of  espousing his cause by challenging the speaking order dated
30.06.2012. 
7.  Thus, cumulatively the delay and laches in the instant case has
remained unexplained. As such, even the principles enunciated by this
Court in the matter of Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag & Anr.  v. Mst.
Katiji & Ors.,  reported in AIR 1987 SC 1353, would also not come to the
rescue of the appellant. For the aforestated commulative reasons, we find
that the impugned order of the learned Single Judge which discloses the
petition having been dismissed on the ground of delay and laches,
affirmed by the Division Bench, would not warrant our interference. Hence,
for the reasons aforestated the appeals stand dismissed.

3. The appellants have moved this Court against the order dated
17.04.2023  passed  by  the  National  Consumer  Dispute  Redressal
Commission at New Delhi (for short “NCDRC”) in Miscellaneous
Application No. 106 of 2021 in Consumer Complaint No. 202 of 2010.
4. Learned  Senior  AAG  for  the  appellants  submit  that  the
respondent has misused the process of the Court and the NCDRC. It
was contended that the plot in question was sold in auction to a

--- Page 201 ---
2
third party from whom the respondent had  purchased it for  a
commercial purpose.
5. It was contended that when the respondent moved the Authority
concerned for grant of a Completion Certificate of his project, the
same was refused primarily on the ground that there were zoning
violations which were of a nature which could not be condoned or
compounded.  However,  it  was  submitted  that  surprisingly,  the
respondent moved before the NCDRC which, by a detailed and reasoned
order dated 01.02.2016, passed by a quorum of two Members of the
NCDRC, had dismissed the claim, holding that the respondent was not
a consumer in view of the matter  relating to purchase of a
commercial plot in a public auction and rejection of the Occupancy
Certificate in respect of a commercial building constructed on such
plot.
6. Learned counsel submitted that there was no infirmity in the
order and the respondent had also accepted the same as for five
years,  he  did  not  move  against  the  said  order.  However,
surprisingly, according to the learned counsel, in the year 2021
M.A. No. 106 of 2021 was filed for Direction in the said case,
which already stood disposed of. The said M.A. was pending and in
the meantime, this Court in CA No. 236 of 2022 by order dated
07.01.2022 had observed that such M.A. would not be maintainable
before the NCDRC in a disposed of matter. It was contended that
despite all this, by the impugned order, the order dated 01.02.2016
was recalled, the  M.A. filed by the respondent was allowed and
consequently the earlier order dated 01.02.2016 was recalled and a

--- Page 202 ---
3
direction  was  issued  to  the  Authorities  to  issue
Occupancy/Completion Certificate to the respondent.
7. Learned counsel submitted that the order is in the teeth of
not only statutory provisions, but also the order of this Court in
CA No. 236 of 2022. It was further contended that even on facts,
because  of  there  being  violation  of  zoning  regulations,  no
indulgence can be shown to the respondent.
8. Learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the NCDRC in
its order dated 01.02.2016, had erroneously held that it was a
commercial transaction and the respondent was not a consumer,
whereas the fact is that he is a consumer as ultimately, it is to
individual parties that the built up space has been sold and thus
the respondent can act on their behalf in representative capacity.
9. While winding up his argument, the learned counsel for the
respondent submitted that as of now, there is a scheme floated by
the State of Haryana under which the prayer of the respondent can
be considered under which he has already applied.
10. Having considered the matter, we find that the order impugned
dated 01.02.2016, passed by the NCDRC in Consumer Case No. 202 of
2010, is well reasoned and did not suffer from any infirmity, much
less could have been reversed on the basis of a Miscellaneous
Application filed by the respondent. Further, we find that the
cause  of  action  to  the  respondent  against  the  order  dated
01.02.2016, not being agitated before the appropriate forum for
five years itself was a ground for his M.A. to be rejected

--- Page 203 ---
4
outright. We also note here that in the M.A., the reliefs claimed
for are substantially new and different from what was the original
prayer made in Consumer Case No. 202 of 2010.
11. Thus, we find that the very inception of the proceedings,
which was before the NCDRC was misconceived.
12. Accordingly, for the reasons aforesaid, the appeal is allowed.
The  order  impugned  dated  17.04.2023  passed  by  the  NCDRC  in
Miscellaneous Application No. 106 of 2021 in Consumer Complaint No.
202 of 2010 is set aside. The order of the NCDRC dated 01.02.2016
in Consumer Case No.202 of 2010 stands revived.
13. It shall be open to the respondent to move before the
appropriate forum, in accordance with law, for any grievance he may
have which shall be considered on its own merit, in accordance with
law.
14. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 4216  OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 16527/2026)
                              (@ DIARY NO.21024/2018)
SHIVDAYAL KOL                                      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH                        RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the appellant and learned counsel
appearing for the respondent-State.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of the impugned judgment and
order dated 18.04.2018 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh,
Principal Seat at Jabalpur in Criminal Appeal No. 883 of 2015,
whereby the appeal preferred by the appellant under Section 374(2)
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, challenging the judgment
of conviction dated 13.03.2015 passed by the learned 5 th Additional
Sessions Judge, Rewa in Sessions Trial No. 244 of 2014, came to be
dismissed. 
4. By the judgment dated 13.03.2015, the learned Trial Court
convicted the appellant for an offence punishable under Section
376(1) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and sentenced him to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for seven years and to pay a fine of
Rs.1,000/-, and in default of payment of fine, to undergo further
rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant was, however,

--- Page 207 ---
2
acquitted of the charge under Section 366 of the Indian Penal Code.
5. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that though the
conviction was recorded on the basis of the evidence led during the
trial, subsequently thereto, an affidavit of the prosecutrix dated
21.09.2015 was placed before the High Court, wherein she had taken
a stand which, according to learned counsel, materially affected
the basis of the prosecution case and the conviction of the
appellant. It is submitted that, in the said affidavit, the
prosecutrix had made categorical assertions which, according to the
appellant, exonerated him of any wrongdoing, much less any criminal
offence, and materially supported the appellant's case that the
relationship between the parties was consensual and that there was
no deception or false assurance of marriage as alleged by the
prosecution. Learned counsel submits that the said material was
placed before the High Court during the pendency of the criminal
appeal and, being relevant to the controversy, ought to have been
considered while deciding the appeal.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the appeal
before  the  High  Court  was  a  continuation  of  the  original
proceedings and, therefore, the High Court ought to have considered
the subsequent material placed before it in accordance with law.
However, it is contended that, in the entire order, there is not
even a reference to the said affidavit, which completely negates
the  charge  against  the  appellant.  It  is  contended  that  the
prosecutrix has cogently explained why she filed the affidavit
after such a long period, which the Court was obliged to consider
and apply its mind to before taking a final call. Learned counsel

--- Page 208 ---
3
further submits that, even in the larger interest of justice, the
Court ought to have taken into consideration such affidavit and its
contents.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent-State submits that the
affidavit was never part of the record before the Trial Court. It
was further submitted that such affidavit is totally contrary to
the deposition of the prosecutrix during the trial before the
Court.
8. In such view of the matter, according to learned counsel for
the  respondent-State,  the  subsequent  affidavit  was  not  even
required to be looked into, and rightly the High Court did not deal
with the same.  
9. At this juncture, on a query of the Court to the learned
counsel for the respondent-State as to why the High Court had not
dealt with the said affidavit and further as to what restriction
existed on the jurisdiction of the High Court to consider such
material treating the same as additional evidence, learned counsel
was not able to satisfy the Court with regard to why the same has
not been done.
10. On a further query of the Court as to whether the State had
filed  any  objection  with  regard  to  the  authenticity  of  the
affidavit of the prosecutrix, the answer was again in the negative. 
11. We have considered the issue in depth. Taking an overall view
of the entire matter and the fact that the prosecutrix herself has
exonerated the appellant of any wrongdoing or of misleading her,
and has clarified that the relationship was consensual, while also

--- Page 209 ---
4
giving an explanation which, in the opinion of the Court, cannot be
said to be frivolous, unacceptable, or unbelievable, and further
noting that the prosecutrix has moved on in life, we deem it fit to
interfere.
12. We note that, in the present case, the dispute is not of such
a nature where it constitutes an offence against the public at
large, but was confined to a relationship between two individuals
who were majors.
13. Thus,  on  an  overall  circumspection  of  the  facts  and
circumstances of the present case, we find that the High Court was
required to deal with the affidavit filed by the prosecutrix before
it.
14. As the said affidavit has, till date, not been controverted or
denied, nor any objection has been taken with regard to its
contents by the State, we can only presume that the affidavit and
its contents are correct.
15. For the reasons aforesaid, the appeal is allowed on the
peculiar facts of the present case. The judgment and order dated
18.04.2018 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Principal
Seat at Jabalpur in Criminal Appeal No. 883 of 2015, as well as the
judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 13.03.2015
passed by the learned 5th Additional Sessions Judge, Rewa in
Sessions  Trial  No.  244  of  2014,  insofar  as  the  appellant's
conviction under Section 376(1) of the IPC is concerned, are set
aside. The appellant stands acquitted of the said charge.

--- Page 210 ---
5
16. The appellant is discharged from the liability of his bail
bonds.
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

              (AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH)
......................J.

1. The  present  civil  appeals  are  arising  out  of  the  judgment  dated
12.11.2013 passed by the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in
Tara Chand (D) by LRs. & Ors. v. Vidya Dhar & Anr.   The dispute involved in the
matter was a five decade old dispute and as many as there are 39 parties to the
dispute.  This Court in order to resolve the dispute amicably has referred the
matter for mediation and finally a mediation report dated 09.01.2026 has been
submitted reflecting that the settlement has been arrived at between 39
persons who are parties to the present litigation.
2. The parties have been allotted respective shares in the property which is
subject matter of the litigation and a Settlement Agreement dated 07.01.2026
has been arrived at between the parties.  The Settlement Agreement has been
signed by the parties as well as by the respective counsels and the same is
annexed herewith as Annexure-A.  The parties to the dispute have been allotted
shares as per the Settlement Agreement and each of them has voluntarily
accepted the Settlement Agreement without any coercion and undue influence.
In order to ensure that the individuals are placed in possession of the respective

--- Page 226 ---
3
shares, copies of two Site Plans have also been filed along with I.A. No. 72997 of
2026 and the same are annexed herewith as Annexure-B.  
3. In the light of the settlement arrived at between the parties, the lis has
come to an end.  Accordingly, the decree passed by the second Appellate Court
is modified in terms of the Settlement Agreement dated 07.01.2026 and in
terms of the Site Plans.  The Settlement Agreement arrived at between the
parties shall be binding upon the parties and all the Civil Appeals stand
disposed of in terms of the Settlement Agreement (Annexure-A) and the Site
Plans (Annexure-B).  A decree shall be drawn, accordingly.  The Settlement
Agreement (Annexure-A) and the Site Plans (Annexure-B) shall form part of the
decree. 
4. This Court also appreciates the efforts on the part of Ms. Manjula Gupta,
Mediator as well as Ms. Sasmita Tripathy and Mrs. Dipa Dixit, the co-Mediators
in assisting the parties to resolve their disputes amicably.  It was their hard
work and persuasive skill which has resulted in positive results; a litigation
which was going on between the parties for the last 50 years has come to an
end amicably.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
 CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1031-1032 OF 2021
THE STATE OF KARNATAKA                      APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
SIDDANNA                                   RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present appeal arises out of the impugned
judgment and order dated 05.12.2017 passed by the High
Court of Karnataka, Kalaburagi Bench, in Crl.R.C. No.
20001/2017,  connected  with  Criminal  Appeal  No.
3623/2012, whereby the High Court rejected Crl.R.C. No.
20001/2017 and consequently allowed Criminal Appeal No.
3623/2012 filed by the respondent, thereby acquitting
the respondent herein of the charge under Section 302
of the IPC.
2. The facts of the case reveal that a case was
registered for offences punishable under Sections 302,
398 and 201 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860, against four accused persons. As one of
them was absconding, the trial was split up and the
trial took place against the remaining three accused
persons.  The  Trial  Court,  vide judgment  dated
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1031-1032 OF 2021

--- Page 231 ---
2
30.06.2012 and order on sentence dated 02.07.2012,
acquitted  two  accused  persons  and  convicted  the
respondent herein.  As per the prosecution case, the
deceased,  Shivakumar  Hiremath , was waiting for some
transport at Tavaragera Bus Stand to go to Lingasugur.
At that point in time, at about 09:30 p.m., a Tata Sumo
vehicle  came,  in  which  four  accused  persons  were
travelling, and they gave a lift to the deceased,
Shivakumar  Hiremath . However, while the vehicle was
moving, Accused Nos.1 and 2 strangulated the deceased
with a rope, Accused No.3 was holding his legs, and
Accused No.4 was driving the said vehicle. The Trial
Court,  after  considering  the  evidence  on  record,
convicted  only  the  present  respondent  herein  and
awarded the death sentence to him. The conviction by
the Trial Court was based upon the recovery of a mobile
phone from PW-11,  Shankaragouda, who stated in his
deposition that the mobile phone belonging to the
deceased, Shivakumar Hiremath , had been sold to him by
the respondent herein,  Siddanna. The evidence also
reveals that some phone calls were made after the
incident from the said mobile phone by the respondent-
accused, not immediately after the incident but at a
later stage, by using his own SIM card. The High Court,
after  examining  the  entire  evidence  on  record,
acquitted the respondent by holding that his conviction
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1031-1032 OF 2021

--- Page 232 ---
3
could not be based solely on the recovery of a mobile
phone from PW-11,  Shankaragouda. It is pertinent to
note that the witnesses to the seizure memo also turned
hostile  during  the  trial,  and  except  PW-11,
Shankaragouda, who reportedly stated before the Trial
Court that he had purchased a mobile phone from the
respondent  herein,  Siddanna,  there  was  no  other
evidence to establish that the mobile phone in question
originally belonged to the deceased. The High Court
held that the recovery, which was not proved, could not
have been made the sole basis for convicting a person
for the offence of murder, especially in light of the
fact that two other accused persons were given a clean
chit by the Trial Court, who were travelling along with
the accused and the deceased and against whom the
allegation  was  that  they  had  caught  hold  of  the
deceased while he was being murdered. No appeal was
preferred  against  the  acquittal  of  the  two  other
accused persons, who were also charged with the offence
under Section 302 of the IPC.
3. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties
at length, this Court is of the considered opinion that
the view expressed by the High Court, based upon the
evidence on record, acquitting the respondent herein
does not warrant any interference. The appeals are,
accordingly, dismissed.
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1031-1032 OF 2021

1. Leave granted. 
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties. 
3. This appeal arises from an interim order
dated  23.04.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Karnataka  at  Bengaluru  in  Criminal  Appeal  No.
739/2026  whereby  while  suspending  the  sentence
awarded by the appellate court, the High Court laid
a condition of depositing Rs.25 lacs which is 50% of
the cheque amount.
4. The submission on behalf of the appellant is
that this is a case where the appellate court had
reversed the acquittal by the trial court and the
mandate of Section 148 is in respect of 20% of
fine/compensation besides once there had been an
acquittal and the judgment is of reversal, there was
no justification to impose an onerous condition.
5. Having regard to the submissions made before
1

--- Page 236 ---
us,  on  26.05.2026  we  had  passed  the  following
interim order:
“1. The submission of the learned
counsel for the petitioner is that
the  trial  court  acquitted  the
petitioner upon finding that the
cheque was not in respect of a
legally  enforceable  debt  as  the
same was time barred.
2. The Appellate Court reversed the
acquittal.
3.  Against  the  order  of  the
Appellate Court, the appellant has
preferred an appeal before the High
Court which is pending.
4. The grievance of the petitioner
is that High Court has directed
deposit  of  50%  of  the  fine  /
compensation even though the facts
of the case did not warrant deposit
and, in any case, deposit ought not
to have been higher than 20%.
5.  Issue  notice,  returnable  in
eight weeks.
6. In the meantime, the petitioner
shall  deposit  20%  cent  of  the
fine / compensation in place of 50%
2

--- Page 237 ---
as directed by the High Court. 5.
Such amount may be deposited in the
Registry  of  the  High  Court  by
30.06.2026. The same shall abide
the result of this petition.”
6. Pursuant  to  the  interim  order  dated
26.05.2026, the appellant has deposited 20% of the
fine/compensation on 29.06.2026 in the registry of
the High Court of Karnataka.
7. The  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant
submits that he has complied with the condition of
deposit.
8. The learned counsel for the respondent does
not dispute the same.
9. Having regard to the above, we dispose of
this appeal by making the interim order absolute.
10. In terms of the above, the interim order
passed by the High Court shall stand modified to the
extent  that  the  deposit  condition  shall  stand
reduced from 50% to 20%.
11. Before parting, we would request the High
Court  to  consider  whether  an  appeal  would  be
maintainable  against  an  order  of  the  appellate
court. The High Court would also consider whether
the appropriate remedy would be a revision.
12. With the aforesaid directions, this appeal
3

THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No(s).  11812-11813/2025
VIMAL S/O LATE SHRI RAMSHANKAR RAGHUVANSHI             Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
ABBOTT HEALTHCARE PVT. LTD & ORS.  
R-1: Abbott Healthcare Pvt. Ltd.,
Managing Director               
R-2: Labour Commissioner, M.G. Road, Indore
R-3: Labour Court, M.G. Road, Indore 
          Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Heard the appellant in person and Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, and Mr.
C.U. Singh, learned Senior Counsel for the respondent No.1.
2. The appellant has assailed the order passed by the High Court,
which ultimately has held that the appellant is not entitled to
invoke the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 on the
basis of being a workman.
3. The matters were heard at length both yesterday and today.
4. Having examined the matters in their entirety, we find that
some issues raised by the appellant, especially with regard to the
provisions of the Sales Promotion Employees (Conditions of Service)
Act, 1976, clearly placing him in the category of a workman or an
1

--- Page 285 ---
 2
employee within and amenable to the provisions of the Industrial
Disputes Act, 1947 have not been considered . Other issues of law
and facts have also been canvassed before us, but in view of the
order we propose to pass, we deem it appropriate not to go into the
same.
5. Accordingly, we find that neither the High Court nor the
Labour Court has taken note of the aforesaid provision, and also
there is no proper consideration of the facts as well.
6. Accordingly, the appeals are disposed of by setting aside the
order of the Labour Court as well as the order of the High Court.
The  matters  are  remanded  to  the  Labour  Court  for  fresh
consideration on all issues of law as well as on facts.
7. Consequently, the proceedings shall stand revived to its
original filing, i.e., Case No. 149/IDR/2017 before the Labour
Court, Indore. The parties shall appear before the Labour Court,
Indore on 28.09.2026.
8. The Labour Court would hear the matters de novo without being
influenced or prejudiced by any observations or findings recorded
either in the earlier order passed by the Labour Court or in the
order of the High Court.
9. We further request the Labour Court to dispose of the matters
expeditiously and latest within 6 months from the date the parties
appear before it. We clarify that we have not expressed any opinion
on the merits of the matters.
10. The Registry is directed to transmit the order to the Labour
2

--- Page 286 ---
 3
Court concerned for necessary action. The parties shall also appear
before the Labour Court along with a copy of the order.
11. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

Delhi.  The  petitioner-company  submitted  a  technical  bid.
However,  on  21.11.2025  the  respondent  no.1  rejected  the
technical bid of the petitioner-company stating : “Others-
blacklisted”.
3. According to the respondent no.1, since the petitioner-
company submitted its bid for a list of 38 drugs including the
drug ““Vitamin A Palmitate Arachis Oil based liquid” which
drug had admittedly being blacklisted qua the petitioner-
company by office order dated 06.10.2023 made by Uttar Pradesh
Medical Supplies Corporation Limited, it’s bid was shown as
“Others-blacklisted”.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that though
in the list of 38 drugs, the said blacklisted drug was
mentioned, the price bid was quoted only for 37 drugs and no
price bid was quoted for the blacklisted drug.
5. We are of the opinion that on facts vis-a-vis the tender
dated 12.06.2025 a decision of the respondent no.1 to treat
the bid of the petitioner as non-responsive was correct. On
this score, the order/judgment of the High Court does not call
for any interference from this Court.
6. At this stage, learned counsel for the petitioner-company
inviting  our  attention  to  paragraph  6  of  the  impugned
order/judgment of the High Court, expresses an apprehension
that the petitioner-company will be treated as blacklisted

--- Page 294 ---
3
from  bidding  forever  only  because  one  of  the  drugs  was
blacklisted with effect from 06.10.2023 for a period of three
years.
7. We find that the said apprehension is not justified.
8. Ms. Swati Ghildiyal, learned counsel for the respondent
no.1 undertakes/states that unless the tender conditions so
provide, the respondent(s) will not treat the petitioner-
company as disqualified from bidding or treat them/him as
blacklisted only because one drug had been blacklisted.
9. Even otherwise we find that blacklisting order was of
06.10.2023 and was for a period of three years and that period
is expiring on 05.10.2026, which is hardly about three weeks
away from today.
10. Under these circumstances, we hold that no case for
interference under Article 136 of the Constitution of India,
is made out.
11. The  tender  process  is  already  concluded  and  as  the
counter  affidavit  indicates,  the  tender  has  already  been
awarded  on  12.12.2025  to  59  companies  for  235  quotes
medicines.
12. Insofar as the apprehension of the petitioner-company
about blacklisting is concerned, our above observations takes
care of the same.
13. With these observations, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.

--- Page 295 ---
4
14. Pending application(s),if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

                                VERSUS
STATE OF U.P. & ORS.                      Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.  
2. The present appeal arises out of judgment and
order dated 16.12.2025 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench in Special
Appeal No.309 of 2024.
3. The order passed  by the High Court relates to
the elections that have been held way back in 2009.
The Committee that has been elected in 2009 would have
demitted its office in 2014.  We are informed that
subsequently, elections were held in 2014 and 2019.
Under aforesaid circumstances, we are of the opinion
that the order passed by the High Court remanding the
case  back  to  learned  Single  Judge  is  totally
unnecessary, as the challenge, if any, to the actions
taken with respect to 2009 elections would have become
infructuous.
4. In this  view of the matter, the judgment and
order  passed  by the High Court is set aside. We make
contd..

--- Page 329 ---
- 2 -
it  clear  that  disputes  relating  to  subsequent
elections, if any, pending before any forum will be
decided on its own merits. 
5. The appeal is according allowed.
